Three of these survive without gravity; **buoyancy** does not, because it is caused by
gravity.
**Step 1 — see where upthrust comes from.** Archimedes' thrust arises because pressure
in a fluid **increases with depth**:
P = hρg ✓
The pressure on the bottom of an immersed body exceeds that on its top, and the
difference is the upward thrust - equal to the weight of fluid displaced:
F = **Vρg** ✓
**Step 2 — set g to zero.** Both the pressure gradient and the thrust vanish:
F = Vρ(0) = **0** ✓
There is no "up" and no "down" for the pressure to vary along. So Archimedes' upward
thrust **would not exist**.
**Step 3 — check the other three.**
**viscosity** ✓ remains - it is internal friction between fluid layers in **relative
motion**, a molecular property quite independent of gravity.
**surface tension** ✓ remains - it comes from the unbalanced cohesive forces on
molecules at the surface. Indeed it becomes **more** prominent without gravity: liquids
in orbit form perfect spheres, because nothing flattens them.
**pressure** ✓ remains - a gas in a sealed container exerts pressure through molecular
bombardment, with or without gravity. What disappears is only the **variation** of
pressure with depth.
**What happens to fluids in free fall.** Everything becomes **neutrally buoyant** ✓
Bubbles no longer rise, sediment no longer settles, and convection stops entirely -
which is why candles burn as dim spheres in orbit and why astronauts drink through
straws rather than pouring.
**Why this matters scientifically.** Many processes on Earth are masked by buoyancy ✓
Crystal growth, alloy mixing and protein crystallisation are all studied in orbit
precisely because sedimentation and convection are absent there.
**The distinction worth keeping.** Pressure itself is a **molecular** effect;
**hydrostatic** pressure variation is a gravitational one ✓ Only the second disappears.
**Reading the distractors.** Each of viscosity, surface tension and pressure has a
molecular origin that gravity plays no part in ✓ Only the upthrust is written with a g
in its formula.
∴ Archimedes' upward thrust.

A liquid crystal has the **fluidity of a liquid** but retains some of the **molecular
order of a crystal**.
**Step 1 — recall the two extremes.**
a **crystalline solid** has long-range order in **position and orientation**, and does
not flow ✓
an **amorphous liquid** has **no** long-range order at all, and flows freely ✓
**Step 2 — place the liquid crystal between them.** Its rod-shaped molecules keep a
common **orientation** - they point roughly the same way - while their **positions**
are disordered, so the material still flows ✓ That is a genuine intermediate, or
**mesophase**.
**Step 3 — conclude.** A liquid crystal is intermediate between a **crystalline solid
and an amorphous liquid** ✓
**The main types.**
**nematic**: molecules aligned in direction but positionally random - the kind used in
displays ✓
**smectic**: aligned **and** arranged in layers, which can slide over one another
**cholesteric**: a twisted nematic whose alignment rotates through the material,
producing the iridescent colours of some beetles and thermometers ✓
**Why they matter.** The **liquid crystal display** ✓ An applied voltage rotates the
molecules, changing how they twist the polarisation of light passing through; crossed
polarisers then turn that twist into brightness. Because the molecules merely rotate,
very little power is needed - which is why LCDs dominate watches, calculators, phones
and screens.
**How they were discovered.** In 1888 the botanist Friedrich Reinitzer found that
cholesteryl benzoate had **two** melting points - turning cloudy at 145 °C and clear at
179 °C ✓ The cloudy phase in between was the first liquid crystal.
**Where they occur naturally.** Cell membranes, DNA solutions, soap films and spider
silk all show liquid-crystalline ordering ✓ Living matter uses the combination of
order and fluidity constantly.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Crystalline solid and vapour**" ✗ names the sublimation
route, with no intermediate phase. "**Amorphous liquid and its vapour**" ✗ describes a
fluid near its critical point. "**A crystal immersed in a liquid**" ✗ is a suspension,
not a phase ✓
∴ crystalline solid and amorphous liquid.

Combining eight drops conserves **volume** and **charge**, so work out the new radius
first.
**Step 1 — find the big drop's radius.** Volume is conserved:
(4/3)πR³ = 8 x (4/3)πr³
R³ = 8r³
**R = 2r** ✓
**Step 2 — find the big drop's charge.** Charge is conserved:
**Q = 8q** ✓
**Step 3 — write the potential of each.**
small drop: V_s = kq/r
big drop: V_b = kQ/R = k(8q)/(2r) = **4(kq/r) = 4V_s** ✓
**Step 4 — solve.**
20 = 4V_s
**V_s = 5 V** ✓
**Why the potential multiplies by 4 and not by 8.** The charge rises eightfold but the
radius doubles, and V = kQ/R, so the ratio is 8/2 = **4** ✓ Combining n drops always
multiplies the potential by **n^(2/3)**, and 8^(2/3) = 4.
**A check with actual numbers.** Take q = 1 nC and r = 1 mm:
V_s = (9 x 10⁹)(10⁻⁹)/10⁻³ = **9000 V**
R = 2 mm, Q = 8 nC
V_b = (9 x 10⁹)(8 x 10⁻⁹)/(2 x 10⁻³) = **36000 V** ✓ exactly four times.
**Why volumes add but radii do not.** Volume is the conserved physical quantity when
liquid merges ✓ and V ∝ R³, so radii combine as cube roots: R = n^(1/3) r.
**The capacitance view.** An isolated sphere has C = 4πε₀R, so the big drop's
capacitance is **twice** each small one's, while it holds **eight** times the charge ✓
V = Q/C then gives the factor of four directly.
**What happens to the energy.** U = Q²/(2C), so
eight separate drops: 8 x (q²/2C_s) = **4q²/C_s**
one big drop: (8q)²/(2 x 2C_s) = **16q²/C_s** ✓
The energy has **quadrupled** - the work being done against the mutual repulsion as the
drops are forced together.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·5 V** ✗ divides by 8, treating the radius as unchanged.
**10 V** ✗ divides by 2, forgetting the charge. **7·5 V** ✗ matches no factor ✓
∴ 5 V.

A thermodynamic coordinate is a **state variable** of the system; the gas constant is a
universal **constant**.
**Step 1 — recall what a thermodynamic coordinate is.** It is a measurable property
that specifies the **state** of a system and changes as the state changes ✓ **Pressure**,
**volume** and **temperature** all qualify - which is why a gas's state is written
(P, V, T).
**Step 2 — look at R.** The universal gas constant is **8·314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹** ✓ It is the
**same for every gas, in every state, at all times**. It does not describe the system -
it is a constant of nature appearing in the equation that relates the real coordinates.
**Step 3 — conclude.** **R is not a thermodynamic coordinate** ✓
**How the coordinates relate to each other.** The equation of state
PV = nRT ✓
links the three, so only **two** are independent for a fixed amount of gas. Fix P and V
and T follows.
**Why R appears at all.** It is the constant of proportionality discovered empirically
by combining Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws ✓ Its value depends only on the
units chosen, not on the gas.
**Other state functions, for contrast.** **Internal energy U**, **entropy S**,
**enthalpy H** and **free energy G** are all state functions too ✓ Each is fixed once
the coordinates are fixed, and each changes when the state does - unlike R.
**What is **not** a state function.** **Heat Q** and **work W** ✓ They depend on the
**path** taken between states, not merely on the endpoints - which is why the first law
is written ΔU = Q − W, with a state function on the left and path quantities on the
right.
**The link between R and k.**
R = N_A k ✓
where k = 1·38 x 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ is Boltzmann's constant. Both are fundamental constants,
and neither describes any particular system.
**Reading the distractors.** **Pressure**, **volume** and **temperature** ✗ are the
three classic thermodynamic coordinates of a gas - the axes of every P-V and P-T
diagram ✓
∴ Gas constant (R).

The drop hangs in equilibrium, so the **electric force balances its weight** - Millikan's
experiment in miniature.
**Step 1 — write the balance condition.**
qE = mg ✓
**Step 2 — express the field through the plate voltage.**
E = V/d ✓
**Step 3 — combine and solve for q.**
q(V/d) = mg
**q = mgd/V** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
q = (10⁻⁶)(10)(10⁻³)/500
= 10⁻⁸/500
= **2 x 10⁻¹¹ C** ✓
**Why the separation is needed.** The plates' potential difference does not by itself
give the field - the **gap** matters ✓ Here E = 500/10⁻³ = **5 x 10⁵ V m⁻¹**, a strong
field, and q = mg/E = 10⁻⁵/(5 x 10⁵) = 2 x 10⁻¹¹ C ✓ the same answer by a second route.
**How many electrons that is.**
n = 2 x 10⁻¹¹/1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ = **1·25 x 10⁸** ✓ about a hundred million excess electrons -
large by atomic standards, but a very small charge in laboratory terms.
**The historical significance.** This is exactly **Millikan's oil-drop experiment** ✓
By balancing charged droplets against gravity he found that every measured charge was a
whole-number multiple of **1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ C**, establishing that charge is **quantised**
and measuring e for the first time. He received the Nobel Prize in 1923.
**Why oil rather than water.** Oil does not **evaporate** appreciably during the
measurement, so the droplet's mass stays constant ✓ Water drops shrink as one watches,
and the balance drifts.
**A check on the units.**
[mgd/V] = (kg)(m s⁻²)(m)/(V) = J/V = **C** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **2 x 10⁻⁹ C** ✗ and **2 x 10⁻⁸ C** ✗ are a hundred and a
thousand times too large - they come from mishandling the millimetre. **2 x 10⁻⁶ C** ✗
is larger still ✓ Keeping d = 10⁻³ m is the step that fixes the power of ten.
∴ 2 × 10⁻¹¹ C.

The **Reynolds number** decides whether flow is smooth or turbulent, and streamline flow
corresponds to **low** values.
**Step 1 — recall the definition.**
Re = ρvD/η ✓
a **dimensionless** ratio of inertial forces to viscous forces.
**Step 2 — recall the ranges.**
**Re < 1000**: flow is **streamline** (laminar) - the layers slide smoothly past one
another ✓
**1000 to 2000**: an unstable transition region
**Re > 2000**: flow becomes **turbulent**, with eddies and chaotic mixing ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** The flow is streamline when **Re is less than 1000** ✓
**What the number is physically comparing.** Viscous forces **damp out** disturbances;
inertial forces **amplify** them ✓ When viscosity dominates - a small Re - any
perturbation dies away and the flow stays orderly. When inertia dominates, perturbations
grow into turbulence.
**Why it is dimensionless.**
[ρvD/η] = (kg m⁻³)(m s⁻¹)(m)/(kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹) = **1** ✓
This is what makes the number universal: the same critical value applies to water in a
pipe, air over a wing and blood in an artery, whatever their sizes.
**Worked examples.**
blood in a capillary: Re ≈ **0·001** - utterly laminar ✓
water in a household pipe: Re ≈ **10⁴** - turbulent
an aircraft wing: Re ≈ **10⁷** - strongly turbulent
**Why turbulence matters.** Turbulent flow mixes far better but dissipates much more
energy ✓ Pipelines are designed to stay laminar where possible, while combustion
chambers are designed to be turbulent, so that fuel and air mix.
**A caution about the exact figures.** The transition is gradual and depends on the
geometry and on how smooth the pipe is ✓ Textbooks quote 1000, 2000 or 2300 for the
critical value; this question uses the lower convention.
**Reading the distractors.** **Greater than 1000** ✗ is the transition or turbulent
region. **2000 to 3000** ✗ and **4000 to 5000** ✗ are firmly turbulent ✓
∴ less than 1000.

A hydraulic lift multiplies force by transmitting pressure undiminished - which is
**Pascal's law**.
**Step 1 — state the law.** Pressure applied to an enclosed incompressible fluid is
transmitted **undiminished to every part** of the fluid and to the walls of the
container ✓
**Step 2 — apply it to the lift.** With a small piston of area a and a large one of
area A sharing the same fluid,
P = F/a = W/A ✓
so
**W = F(A/a)** ✓
A small force on the narrow piston raises a large load on the wide one.
**Step 3 — note what is not gained.** The **work** is the same at both ends ✓
F x (distance moved by small piston) = W x (distance moved by large piston)
so the small piston must travel **A/a times further**. Force is multiplied; energy is
not created.
**A worked instance.** With a = 1 cm² and A = 100 cm²:
a force of **100 N** lifts **10000 N**, a tonne ✓
but the small piston must descend **100 cm** to raise the load **1 cm**.
**Why the fluid must be incompressible.** A gas would simply compress, absorbing the
motion instead of transmitting it ✓ Hydraulic systems use oil, which is also a
lubricant and does not corrode the cylinders.
**Where else the law is used.** Hydraulic brakes, jacks, presses, excavator arms and
aircraft controls ✓ In a car, pressing one pedal applies equal pressure at all four
wheels - a direct consequence of Pascal's law.
**Why the other laws do not apply.**
**Stokes' law** ✗ gives the viscous drag on a sphere, F = 6πηrv.
**Torricelli's law** ✗ gives the efflux speed from a hole, v = √(2gh).
**Bernoulli's principle** ✗ relates pressure and speed in a **moving** fluid - it
governs aerofoils and venturi meters, but a hydraulic lift works with the fluid
essentially **at rest** ✓
**The statement in its sharpest form.** In a static fluid the pressure at a point acts
**equally in all directions**, and any added pressure appears everywhere at once ✓
∴ Pascal's Law.
